newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghanistan's victorious Taleban face tough task.
newsitem.headline: Afghanistan's victorious Taleban face tough task.

text.p: The collapse of the stronghold of the Afghan opposition and surrounding provinces has left the Taleban in control of 90 percent of Afghanistan but facing the task of rebuilding a society wrecked by almost 20 years of war.
The Taleban's victories leave the opposition in just a few vulnerable bastions in the mountainous northeastern and central regions of the country.
The Taleban, with their radical policy of implementing strict Islamic law, have shown themselves to be formidable fighters, but their ability to run a nation state has yet to be proved.
"They are a revolutionary movement that grew from an overpowering desire to sort out the chaos that engulfed the country after the fall of the communists (in 1992)," said an analyst.

"But now the military threat has receded, it remains to be seen how they are going to maintain their cohesion and change gear to become a civil government," said the analyst, who preferred not to be identified.
Since the Taleban captured Kabul last September, they have ruled the country with an interim council and acting ministers. Many of their policies have been justified by citing "the emergency".

"When we have peace, they will relax their rules and life will get back to normal. The only reason that they have such strict rules is that the security situation is still unclear," one Taleban fighter told Reuters in Kabul shortly before the collapse of the opposition.

But the analyst is less sure. "The Taleban's policy comes from their village roots. There is no middle class left to modify their policies. I think that the Taleban are happy with things the way they are," he said.
When the Taleban first emerged in late 1994, their stated aims were to open the roads, disarm the warring factions and impose their purist vision of Islamic law on the country.
They have expanded little on their policy aims, beyond saying that they do not present a threat to any outside country and saying they will address the problems of peace when it arrives.
They say that they eventually want some kind of representative government, but have yet to clarify how the government will be selected or how it will operate.
The Taleban have yet to be recognised as Afghanistan's legitimate government by any nation or international organisation.

Afghans hope that, whatever the politics of the Taleban, with the new-found security of a unified Afghanistan they will be able to re-open trade routes, particularly between Central Asia and the sub-continent.
With few easily exploitable natural resources, the country has since antiquity made its money from being a crossroads between between East and West.

With the communist invasion in 1979, and then the descent into chaos that occurred after the communist defeat in 1992, trade has been reduced to a trickle. The export of narcotics now ranks as Afghanistan's number one foreign exchange earner.

The Afghans are not the only ones to scent the possibilities of peace. Two oil companies, Unocal of the United States and Bridas of Argentina, are competing to build a $2.5 billion gas pipeline from energy-rich Turkmenistan in the north to Pakistan in the south.
